"I decided to make up a list of AI discourse brainworms:

There are distinctly 3 currently well-represented different mainstream idea spaces. Denialist Anti-AI, X-Risk Anti-AI and Toolism.

*Denialist Anti-AI*: Mainstream opinion that AI is a fake scam technology/slop/will disappear after an economic bubble collapse. Also known as Gebruism to those familiar with its industry/academia origins. Popular among mainstream hard leftists.

*X-Risk Anti-AI*: Distinctly not specifically just rationalism doomers. This is a superset of that, which includes the more popular version, 'Terminator was scary' and less popular versions, such as "computers are the antichrist". Also known, as of this week, to the general populace, as Sandersism (lol). Popular among polyamorous nerds from the West Coast and boomers.

*Toolism*: Mainstream pro-AI opinion, 'it's just a tool', 'the new trains', etc. ... Popular among the apolitical, general techies, casual chatGPT users, small business owners making ugly and confusing food menus."

On this interpretation, what modern philosophy calls the hard problem would be one instance of a pattern something like:

We distinguish A from B for perfectly legitimate practical and explanatory purposes.

We then implicitly convert that distinction into:

A is intrinsically A.
B is intrinsically B.

We then ask:

How could A possibly become B?

And suddenly we have generated an apparently bottomless metaphysical problem.

The Madhyamaka response is not:

> “Here's the mechanism by which A turns into B.”

It's:

> “Examine what you mean by A and B having the independent natures required for that problem to arise.”

And that makes its age more, rather than less, interesting

Normally, saying “someone thought of this 1,800 years ago” isn't powerful evidence. Ancient people had thousands of philosophical ideas; some were insightful and some weren't.

But this case has a somewhat different character.

Nāgārjuna didn't happen to make one lucky observation about consciousness. He developed a systematic method for dealing with precisely this family of apparent ontological oppositions. His surviving arguments date to around the second century CE, and his work became one of the major philosophical traditions of Asia. 

If the same machinery can be brought to bear, without substantial modification, on a problem formulated nearly two millennia later, that's evidence of considerable generality in the framework.

It suggests Nāgārjuna may have identified something about the architecture of metaphysical problems themselves.

That's much more impressive than anticipating one answer.

It would make the hard problem somewhat historically provincial.

Not meaningless, and certainly not unintelligent. But its particular formulation emerges from a philosophical culture strongly shaped by questions like:

mental versus physical
subject versus object
appearance versus reality
intrinsic versus derived properties

Madhyamaka comes at the matter from somewhere quite different. It asks whether either side of such oppositions can withstand analysis as possessing svabhāva in the first place.

And so you get this peculiar situation:

Western philosophy can spend several centuries asking which side is fundamental—

matter?
mind?
both?
something neutral?

—while Madhyamaka's response from ~1,800 years ago is essentially:

You keep changing your candidate for the foundation without examining the assumption that there must be a foundation of that sort.

That is a genuinely radical difference.
